articles.title_zh: China’s ‘mountain of immortals’: why millions flock to the peaks of Wudang
articles.content_orig:
The sacred mountain range dotted with ancient Taoist temples attracts pilgrims and visitors praying for everything from peace to good weather
A banknote clasped between her hands, Liu Haiyan prays to the protector of the Wudang Mountains. The range in central China’s Hubei province has long been considered sacred in Taoism.
“I asked him to bless our motherland with favourable weather and to make it even more prosperous,” Liu says while sitting outside the Golden Hall, a Taoist temple at the summit of Tianzhu Peak.
“This place watches over our country,” she adds. “We’re Chinese, and this is part of our faith.”
Tourists and pilgrims in a steady stream make their way through Wudang every day. Its scenic peaks, ancient palaces and religious sites drew 14 million visits in 2025, according to government figures.

articles.title_orig: Live Updates: Tennessee Inmate in Critical Condition After ‘Torturous’ Botched Execution, Lawyer Says
articles.title_zh: Live Updates: Tennessee Inmate in Critical Condition After ‘Torturous’ Botched Execution, Lawyer Says
articles.content_orig:
What we know about Christa Pikeâs condition after failed execution
Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike is in "critical condition, receiving life-saving care" at hospital, after surviving two lethal injection attempts, leading the state's governor to halt all executions for the year.
"We don't have a sense of her prognosis or much update on her health at the moment," her lawyer Randy Spivey told reporters on Thursday. "But we do know that she is alive right now."
Her lawyers are now asking for her sentence to be commuted. Pike, 50, was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of Colleen Slemmer.
She was injected with two lethal doses of pentobarbital on Wednesday but remained alive, her lawyers said. She was then sent to hospital in an ambulance.
Watch: Witnesses recount Christa Pike's failed execution attempt
Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer.
Her attempted execution on Wednesday was the subject of a last-minute legal battle. This culminated in the US Supreme Court allowing the lethal injections to go ahead.
Slemmer's mother May Martinez, who was among those who wanted the execution to take place and who travelled to Tennessee to witness it, told NBC News after the botched attempt that "it was a mess".
On Thursday afternoon, Pike's lawyers offered more details about what happened during the attempted execution, describing a harrowing scene shrouded in secrecy.
"Last night, the execution team attempted to establish an IV line for an hour," Spivey said. "I counted at least seven needles used in her left arm alone, one of which appeared to be bent when it was pulled from her arm after an unsuccessful attempt."
Spivey said that observers were kept in a dark room behind a closed curtain, after the second lethal dose had been administered and "it was clear that Miss Pike was still breathing" minutes later.
"No-one knew what was going on behind that curtain," Spivey said. "I had no idea when and if medical professionals began to assist."
Spivey said the state's governor must commute Christa's sentence now,  a request that was denied previously.
Stephen Ferrell, another of Pike's lawyers, said they were also looking at other legal options.
"We want to think this through and we want to make sure that Christa recovers and has some input in what she wants," he said.
Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has ordered an independent review and said on Thursday the investigation into Pike's botched execution "will be thorough", adding that "it's going to take time".
"There are a lot of questions," Lee said. "The people of our state deserve to have those questions answered, and that's what this investigation is for."
Lee has not made clear who will conduct the independent review of the state's execution procedures.
His order to pause all executions will overlap with the planned 3 December execution of convicted murderer Gary Sutton.
The Tennessee Department of Correction, which handled the execution, issued a statement defending its handling of the case.
It said in a statement that it "followed every step of the State's lawful, established execution protocol approved by the attorney general's office".
"The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective, and the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out this evening."
Pike was given two doses of the chemical pentobarbital, in accordance with state protocol when the first attempt fails, but was still alive afterwards, according to court filings by her lawyers.
"This execution is causing Ms Pike unnecessary agony and occurring in violation of his right to be executed free of cruel and unusual punishment," her lawyers said.
The Tennessee attorney general's office said in a statement that it agreed with the decision to call for an investigation, adding: "We need to know what happened."
US Republican Senator Marsha Blackburn, who is running for Tennessee governor, described the situation as "tragic".
"While there should be a thorough review of what happened and why the process failed, the answer is simple: bring back the electric chair," Blackburn said.
Democrat Jerri Green, Blackburn's opponent, criticised her for wanting to "bring back one of the most cruel forms of capital punishment".
"As governor, I would put a moratorium on all future executions," Green said on X.
This is the second time in 2026 Tennessee officials attempted and failed to execute a prisoner.
In May, the execution of Tony Carruthers was called off after staff were unable to find a vein to administer a lethal drug. Carruthers was given a year's reprieve.

articles.title_orig: Man Charged With Threatening Katie Miller, Wife of a Top Trump Aide
articles.title_zh: Man Charged With Threatening Katie Miller, Wife of a Top Trump Aide
articles.content_orig:
A Massachusetts man was indicted on Thursday for allegedly cyberstalking podcaster Katie Miller, who is married to White House deputy chief of staff for policy Stephen Miller, according to the Justice Department and sources familiar with the matter.
The indictment charges John Anthony Proia III, 41, of Waltham, with cyberstalking a "former political advisor and prominent member of the Republican party" who is married to a "high-level federal government employee" with more than 40 calls and texts between August and September of this year, the Justice Department said.
The indictment does not name the Millers, but sources familiar with the case confirmed to CBS News that they are the victims in the case.
Katie Miller could not immediately be reached for comment.
On X, she retweeted a post about the case by Attorney General Todd Blanche and wrote, "Thank you Todd Blanche, Leah Foley and the Washington Field Office."
The indictment follows a dust-up at the Washington Field Office of the FBI, which was investigating the alleged threats. Last week, two senior-level counterterrorism FBI agents were demoted from their positions, after the Millers complained that the FBI wasn't doing enough to investigate the harassment.
The demotion was first reported by Bloomberg Law. Darren Cox, who leads the Washington Field Office, later issued a statement saying that he had made the personnel decision, and not FBI Director Kash Patel.
This is at least the second time Katie Miller has asked the FBI to investigate alleged threats or harassment.
Last year, Katie Miller complained to local and federal law enforcement about local activist Barbara Wien after she distributed flyers near the Millers' Arlington, Virginia, home that showed Stephen Miller on a "Wanted" poster for "crimes against humanity."
The flyers contained his Arlington address, and they also provided a QR code that urged people to demand a congressional investigation.
The incident with the protesters prompted the Millers to move into military housing.
A federal investigation into the matter hit a dead end after a magistrate judge twice rejected a search warrant for Wien's phone, CBS News previously reported.
The state investigation into the matter ended earlier this year, after Arlington and Falls Church Commonwealth Attorney Parisa Dehghani-Tafti said in a lengthy court filing that she had reviewed evidence against Barbara Wien and found that "nothing in the proceeds of the search warrant supports criminal prosecution" for violations of a state law that criminalizes using someone's identity or address as a means to coerce, intimidate or harass.
In the case on Thursday, prosecutors said that Proia called multiple times a day using different numbers, and sometimes left voicemails.
The Justice Department said that Proia also contacted Katie Miller's mother and left a number of disturbing text messages, including one that greeted her by name, referred to Stephen Miller as "evil" and used an obscenity.
In another text, he allegedly wrote to Katie Miller's father: "Hey [first name of victim's father], how goes it?  Hope your daughter marrying a Jewish Nazi/white supremacist is working out for you and [first name of victim's mother]."
Proia was due to appear in federal court at 5 p.m. on Thursday. CBS News could not immediately reach his attorney for comment.
Jennifer  Jacobs contributed to this report.

The cause of death for Chad Lowe’s daughter Fiona has been confirmed.
The teenager, who was 13, died by suicide at the hospital on Tuesday, per a report from the medical examiner obtained by Page Six.

articles.title_orig: Global bond rout deepens, pushes US Treasury yields to 24-year peak
articles.title_zh: Global bond rout deepens, pushes US Treasury yields to 24-year peak
articles.content_orig:
Treasury yields fell on Thursday, giving back some of the recent gains that propelled longer-dated rates to levels not seen in decades.
The 10-year Treasury yield breached a level last seen in April 2002, before easing 5 basis points to 5.243%. The 10-year influences rates on mortgage and auto loans and credit card debt. The yield on the 30-year Treasury bond also hit its highest in 24 years before dropping more than 2 basis points to 5.613%.
Yields and prices move inversely. One basis point equals 0.01%.
Jeff Kilburg, CEO of KKM Financial, said he sees the 10-year yield pulling back to around 4.5%-4.75% if the U.S. and Iran can reach a deal to end the war. "If we're going to continue to stay in Iran, then that's going to be problematic for the 10-year yield."
Government borrowing costs around the world continued their relentless march upward on Thursday, continuing a monthslong trend as investors voted with their feet over a lack of political will to tackle fiscal deficits, while inflation remains stubbornly above target and leading central banks move to push interest rates higher.
Major economies face "persistently large deficits and rising interest expenses — challenges long associated with debt-distressed emerging market sovereigns," the Institute of International Finance said last week .
Japan's 10-year yield hit its highest level since the mid-1990s. Japan's debt has come under pressure from a weaker yen and rate hikes by the Bank of Japan .
The yield on the German 10-year bund, the benchmark for the euro area, topped 3.6%, the highest since 2008, before easing back. Elsewhere in Europe, the French 10-year surged 8 basis points to 4.925%, Italy's 10-year was up 10 basis points to 4.706%, while the U.K.'s 10-year yield increased 5 basis points to 5.483%.
"It's worth noting, but people get pretty worked up about those sorts of spreads regularly, so I don't think it's a crisis point necessarily, as far as Germany versus France or Italy," said Michael Schumacher, former managing director at Wells Fargo. "If you look at some countries that have very poor structural dynamics, like the UK, and I'd be concerned about that. People don't typically trade gilts versus bunds as much, but just as a barometer of, say, market concern, I think that's one to watch."
Bonds had been moving in lockstep with oil prices , which have been turbulent as the U.S.-Israel war with Iran obstructed crude exports from the Middle East. Crude oil prices were higher on Thursday , with international benchmark Brent crude futures back above $100 a barrel.
"We could see [bond] buyers come in effectively to take advantage of those yields, which would have the effect of causing them to go down, but also one of the things that has kept the volatility in those yields in the long end of the curve has been what's going on with oil, what's going on with inflation," Nomi Prins, founder of Prinsights Global, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Thursday.
But sovereign wealth funds and central banks, among the main long-term holders of Treasury debt, are unlikely to go along, Prins said.
"We could see movement ... in Treasury yields going down if oil prices go down significantly, if there's a resolution" in the Middle East, Prins added.
— With additional reporting from CNBC's Jeff Cox

articles.title_orig: Judge blocks Trump's firing of top federal prosecutor in Seattle and restores him as U.S. attorney
articles.title_zh: Judge blocks Trump's firing of top federal prosecutor in Seattle and restores him as U.S. attorney
articles.content_orig:
Washington — A federal judge on Thursday blocked President Trump's firing of Roger Rogoff from his post as the top federal prosecutor in Seattle, finding the president cannot unilaterally remove a U.S. attorney who has been tapped to the post by a district court.
U.S. District Judge Stanley Bastian delivered his decision from the bench at the end of a hearing, during which he agreed to grant Rogoff's request to reinstate him until the Senate confirms a replacement. Mr. Trump nominated Simon Peter Serrano to the position of U.S. attorney in Seattle last month.
Bastian ruled that Rogoff is the U.S. attorney in the Western District of Washington and has been the "rightful holder of that office" since July 15, when the federal district judges in the region installed him to the role and he took his oath of office.
Mr. Trump fired Rogoff less than an hour after he was sworn in.
"The real issue to be decided in this case by this court appears to be one of first impression: can the president fire a U.S. attorney appointed by the district court?" Bastian said, later adding, "The answer to the question the court is faced with is no. The president cannot unilaterally fire a United States attorney appointed by the district court."
The Justice Department said it intends to appeal and will immediately seek to halt the ruling.
In addition to declaring Rogoff as the U.S. attorney, Bastian said Charles Neil Floyd, the first assistant who has been leading the office, "is not the United States attorney" for the Western District of Washington, and authority to perform the role's responsibilities was "improperly granted."
Mr. Trump signed an order last week that directed Floyd "to perform the functions and duties of the office of United States Attorney."
"Allowing the president to fire a U.S. attorney appointed by the district court would upend the framework created by the Constitution and the statutes, which together balance the president's right to appoint and the Senate's right to confirm," Bastian said. "Allowing the president to fire a United States attorney appointed by the court also eliminates the incentive to nominate a candidate that can be confirmed by the Senate. In other words, the executive and legislative branches are supposed to and encouraged to work together."
In his oral order, the judge prohibited the Trump administration from putting Rogoff's firing into effect until the U.S. attorney spot is filled by a Senate-confirmed candidate. He also said the administration cannot purport to remove Rogoff from his position, deny him access to benefits or resources of the position, or obstruct Rogoff from his ability to carry out his duties.
Finally, Bastian said the Trump administration cannot treat anyone other than Rogoff as U.S. attorney.
"The court finds it is in the public interest that the law be followed and that Mr. Rogoff take the office to which he has already taken the oath of office," he said.
"I care deeply about the rule of law and the careful checks and balances envisioned by our Founders and carried out by Congress," Rogoff said in a statement provided to CBS News. "I appreciate the judicial process and am now focused on assuming the role of U.S. attorney and getting to work for the people of Western Washington."
The U.S. attorney's office in Seattle has not had a Senate-confirmed leader since mid-2023. After Mr. Trump took office, he fired Tessa Gorman as the top prosecutor in the office. She had been serving temporarily before judges on the district court appointed her to the job in May 2024.
Floyd began leading the office as interim U.S. attorney in October, but his appointment was subject to a 120-day clock, which expired in February. He then began serving as first assistant U.S. attorney, the second-in-command, and said at the time that he would continue leading the office.
Because Mr. Trump had not by that time put forth a nominee to serve as the top federal prosecutor in Seattle, the district judges exercised their authority under a federal law governing U.S. attorney vacancies to tap Rogoff for the job. That law allows the attorney general to appoint an interim U.S. attorney, who is subject to a 120-day term. Once that appointment expires, the district court can either agree to extend that prosecutor's tenure or appoint its own U.S. attorney until the Senate confirms a replacement.
Following his swift firing, Rogoff filed a lawsuit against the Trump administration and argued that his removal was unlawful. He argued that if not blocked by the court, the Trump administration's "actions will permit the Executive Branch to evade the Senate's advice-and-consent role indefinitely."
Mr. Trump has attempted to install his preferred candidates for U.S. attorney in several other places, including Nevada, New York, Virginia and New Jersey. Federal courts have in those instances, some of which involve a slightly different mechanism, found the appointments unlawful.
Rogoff, however, appears to be the first ousted prosecutor to challenge his firing in court.

articles.title_orig: Trump’s Supreme Court grievance grows as new term looms
articles.title_zh: Trump’s Supreme Court grievance grows as new term looms
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — President Trump vented about his three nominees to the Supreme Court in a new interview, calling their rulings on matters such as his tariffs “very disappointing” after “I gave them the position of a lifetime.”
“I put them in. They voted against me too often,” Trump told Time magazine when asked about his previous social media attack on Justices Amy Coney Barrett, Neil Gorsuch and Brett Kavanaugh after the trio voted against the president’s proposed rules for mail-in voting.
“I gave them the position of a lifetime, and they vote against me often. They vote for me too,” he said.
“The Democrats stick like glue — those three, they virtually never vary. You can come up with the worst thing in the world and they’ll vote as a group. And while I don’t like it, there’s something I admire about it: there’s loyalty. So they have loyalty to Barack Hussein Obama,” he added.
“They have loyalty to Biden, even though Biden doesn’t even know who the hell they are. He wouldn’t know. He doesn’t even know what the Supreme Court is. And me, I gave them the chance of a lifetime, and it’s unfortunate what they did.”
Trump mentioned rulings over the past year on tariffs and birthright citizenship.
“I don’t want loyalty. I want good decisions. The tariff decision was disastrous for the country,” he said. “All they had to do was a little clause saying any money paid does not have to be paid back…would have saved $400 billion. They chose not to save that.”
Gorsuch and Barrett voted in February to invalidate Trump’s new 10% baseline tariff for most countries and a levy imposed on China, Mexico and Canada as punishment for fentanyl smuggling — entitling businesses to more than $100 billion in refunds.
“It’s unfortunate what they did—not to me, to our country. Birthright citizenship. It’s becoming a major industry now. People are making millions and millions of dollars, and we’re losing trillions of dollars,” Trump added.
“It’s become a corrupt business, all because of the Supreme Court decision. That decision was for the babies of slaves. Look at where it was—look at where it was approved. It wasn’t for Chinese people, wealthy or unwealthy, coming, you know, pouring into our country.”

Barrett voted with the majority to overturn Trump’s executive order seeking to deny citizen to children of parents who are not citizens or permanent residents. Kavanaugh concurred in part and dissented in part on that ruling.
Trump previously ripped his picks to the high court on Sept. 15, writing on social media that “these are not the people I interviewed.”
However, the hard feelings didn’t prevent Trump from giving away four of just 134 tickets to the Sept. 24 US-China state dinner to Barrett, Kavanaugh and their spouses.

articles.title_orig: Lindsay Clancy lawyer’s bid to get killer mom’s murder charges tossed is slapped down
articles.title_zh: Lindsay Clancy lawyer’s bid to get killer mom’s murder charges tossed is slapped down
articles.content_orig:
Lindsay Clancy’s lawyer lost his fourth attempt to get the murder charges his accused killer mom client faces thrown out Thursday.
Judge William Sullivan denied a motion by Clancy’s lawyer, Kevin Reddington , to have her found not guilty on all three first-degree murder charges after the high-profile case ended in a mistrial on Sept. 4.
Reddington, 75, argued the motion in court Tuesday, questioning the evidence that the 36-year-old mom strangled her three young kids with exercise bands.
“Where is the evidence that she did this?” he asked the court, before insisting, “This entire case is based on speculation.”
But Sullivan ruled in a decision Thursday that prosecutors had presented sufficient evidence at trial of Clancy’s alleged crimes and therefore he couldn’t drop the charges.
“There was evidence introduced, both physical and circumstantial, that would permit a rational trier of fact to find beyond a reasonable doubt the elements of the charge of murder,” the judge declared.
At the six-week-long trial, prosecutors claimed Clancy coldly planned and executed the murders of her kids , Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months, in their Duxbury, Massachusetts, basement on Jan. 24, 2023.
But Reddington asked the jury to find her not guilty by reason of insanity, claiming she was experiencing extreme postpartum psychosis and heard a voice commanding her to kill the kids and herself.
Morning Report delivers the latest news, videos, photos and more.
Reddington previously tried to get his client’s charges dropped three other times — but Sullivan denied every attempt.
The trial ended earlier this month after the jury, made up of nine women and three men, said three times they couldn’t reach a unanimous agreement after seven days of deliberations.
Several of the jurors spoke out publicly after the mistrial was declared and revealed that 11 members of the panel were in favor of finding Clancy not criminally responsible, while a lone holdout wanted to convict her.
Prosecutors haven’t announced how they plan to move forward with the case and a new trial date has yet to be set.
Clancy is due back in court on Nov. 2.
Reddington didn’t immediately return a request for comment Thursday afternoon.

“ Primetime ” is a box office overachiever , but the subject of the A24 film calls it a “complete work of fiction.”
Lance Oppenheim’s movie centers on “To Catch a Predator,” the popular “Dateline” segment that ran from 2004 to 2007. In the show, an advocacy group with adult decoys posing as children would chat with online predators in order to lure them to a house, ostensibly to have sex with a minor. But instead of their prey, they would be met by host Chris Hansen (played by Robert Pattinson), who would interrogate the predators about why they were pursuing illicit and illegal affairs. The suspects were then arrested by law enforcement waiting outside the house.
The film is based more specifically on the 2009 Esquire article “Tonight on ‘Dateline’ This Man Will Die,” which chronicled an episode of the show involving Louis William Conradt Jr., an assistant district attorney in Murphy, Texas, who died by suicide after being caught in a police sting conducted in coordination with the “Predator” team.
Hansen is continuing his work on his media platform, TruBlu , which hosts shows such as the spiritual successor to “Predator,” “Takedown With Chris Hansen,” which launched in 2022.
Variety spoke with Hansen a few days after he watched “Primetime.” He discussed his perspective on its box office success, which parts are most upsetting to his former colleagues and what legal action he might take against A24.
No. The only elements of the movie that are not fictionalized are the fact that he uses my name and two or three catchphrases. Everything else is fictionalized. Yes, there was an assistant DA who tragically took his own life, but the circumstances surrounding it, the timeline, the events, it may be based on reality, but none of it is truthful. It’s a complete work of fiction.
Look, nobody wants to see somebody take their own life. But in this case, you had a public official, an assistant district attorney who prosecuted criminal cases, who, according to the police and evidence gathered in the case, conducted sexually explicit conversations with decoys posing as two different teenage boys. In Texas, like many other states, that constitutes a felony. Now, he didn’t show up at the house, but the police made a decision to get a warrant based on probable cause. And I think if you were to talk to the police making those decisions, they would tell you that there was some concern that evidence might be destroyed and that they were going to go serve that arrest warrant at his home.
Now, obviously, we knew they were gonna do this, and we captured the action from the street. And when they went in, according to Murphy police, he had a gun in his hand. He said, “I’m not going to hurt you guys,” and took his own life. Later, Texas Rangers did an investigation, and they determined that on that computer from which he was trying to extract the hard drive, there was child sexually abusive material. As a prosecutor, he knew that in Texas, you could potentially face 10 years in prison for each of those images. So nobody can tell you exactly why Bill Conradt took his own life. Nobody wanted to see it happen. It’s tragic for his family. It’s tragic for him. But to insinuate that there was some push on our part to go arrest him or get him or to find him or to cajole him, it just didn’t happen. He surfaced like any other alleged predator did in an investigation. The decoys don’t go try to find them. They conduct the investigation, and they find us.
The rules on it are very, very explicit. But we have caught a number of high-profile people. We were in San Francisco on a sting last month, and an Ivy League-educated lawyer who ran a multimillion-dollar investment fund showed up in the middle of the day to sexually exploit a 6- and 13-year-old boy whose father he thought was going to take part in the sex act. We don’t look for people; they find us. The whole premise of the movie is false. It’s a fake narrative. It didn’t happen. If that was the case and the police wanted to make a big splash publicitywise, wouldn’t you think they’d wait till Monday when he was sitting in his office at the district attorney’s office and barge in and get him and walk him out of there? That’s what they would have done. Everybody wants to say that this was done for clicks and ratings, and it wasn’t; it was just part of an investigation.
If anybody would take a moment, as some content creators have, and actually look at the story that we did on that particular case, and look at what we did on “The Today Show” the next morning, we were painstakingly transparent about what happened, how it happened and, as much as we knew, why it happened, as we have been with this franchise from the very beginning, continuing through today when we do these investigations which we now call “Takedown With Chris Hansen.” Any sense that anybody involved was pushing forward or that there was a ratings-hungry producer, none of that is true. Even the notion of the name of the film, “Primetime” — “Dateline” has always been on primetime television. It wasn’t like it was at 2 o’clock in the morning, and we were trying to get it on primetime. It was always on primetime. No discussion in that film ever happened.
There are people who think that we have historically worked too closely with law enforcement. But my argument is that’s the only way to be socially responsible and to ensure that there’s justice served in these cases. In the first two investigations, we didn’t collaborate with law enforcement. We didn’t know what was going to happen, but it became very clear in the third investigation that we needed to have a law enforcement presence. That has evolved over the past 22 years into what I think is the best possible way of doing this. That is to ensure justice and to ensure the chain of custody of evidence is secure. And also, look, it doesn’t matter how horrifying the crime is, everybody in this country is entitled to a vigorous defense. So the materials that we capture, obviously, everybody has access to that. Whether you’re the prosecutor or the defense, everybody deserves their fair day in court.
It’s par for the course. You know, even the filmmakers will tell you that this is fiction. And, you know, even when something reflects potentially a real-life event, the timeline has shifted around to make it work in the narrative of the filmmaker. But again, the timeline and the narrative and all of it is fiction. And so, the motives and everything that is detailed in the film, none of that actually happened the way it’s depicted. For them to do that, what’s the motive of making that film? A lot is being made of that right now. What does that say about Hollywood? If you’re gonna make a fictional film, why do you use my name?
The reason you use it is because I’ve spent 45 years creating a very valuable brand, and they wanted to exploit it. They know that if they use the name “Chris Hansen,” people will come to the movie. Most of them will understand the movie is fiction, and there’s a graphic at the end of the film saying so. But that’s not the way it’s portrayed in the beginning of the film. And because there was such an attempt to imitate — although I think it was way more dramatic and over the top — my mannerisms and my lines and things I’ve said over the years, they turned it into a science fiction film, almost, with the greens and the vampire look of the character. It’s just over the top. In fact, it was so over the top, I was left wondering, “What’s the point of this?” And again, I’m not objective, because they exploited me and my brand and my name image for commercial enterprise. Israel could respond if investigators confirm an Iranian link to the co-pilot accused of trying to crash the Dubai-to-Tel Aviv flight, regional sources told Fox News chief foreign correspondent Trey Yingst.
Reporting on “America Reports,” Yingst said the investigation remained ongoing after President Donald Trump suggested Iran may be connected to the suspect.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu cautioned that it was “too early to say whether he had any connections with Iran or with anyone else.”
Fox News contributor and Hudson Institute senior fellow Rebeccah Heinrichs said a weakened Iranian regime could still inspire or direct violence, while the segment emphasized that no connection had been established.
Heinrichs also praised the passengers and wounded captain who intervened, comparing their courage to Todd Beamer’s actions aboard United Flight 93.
“It’s that kind of courage and behavior that’s really going to save the day,” she said.
She warned against allowing the attack to undermine progress between Israel and the UAE, calling flydubai a symbol of the Abraham Accords.
The airline has suspended flights to and from Israel while authorities investigate.
India’s ambassador to Israel paid tribute to Capt. Smit Machchhar at a gathering in Tel Aviv, praising the wounded pilot’s role in helping save 174 lives aboard flydubai Flight FZ1073.
Ambassador JP Singh honored Machchhar during the India-Israel Festival and National Convention of Indian Jews, India’s embassy in Israel said on X.
Singh said the captain’s bravery had made Israel and the world proud, according to the embassy.
The ambassador also wished Machchhar a speedy and complete recovery following the attack aboard the Dubai-to-Tel Aviv flight.
India’s president praised Capt. Smit Machchhar for protecting passengers despite serious injuries during the attack aboard the Dubai-to-Tel Aviv flight.
“The nation is proud of Captain Smit Machchhar,” the president’s official account wrote on X. “His heroic courage and incredible presence of mind have deeply touched us all.”
The post credited Machchhar’s determination and quick response with helping prevent a major tragedy.
“Even after being seriously injured in a moment of grave peril, he remained determined to protect the lives of others,” the statement read.
Israeli officials have credited the captain with opening the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew to intervene.
“I salute his indomitable spirit,” the president wrote. “I pray for his speedy recovery and good health.”
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi praised Capt. Smit Machchhar for fighting back during the Dubai-to-Tel Aviv flight attack, calling his actions “the highest form of courage.”
“Without fearing for his own life, he fought valiantly and prevented another 9/11 like attack from happening,” Modi wrote on X.
Machchhar has been credited by Israeli officials with opening the cockpit door despite serious injuries, allowing passengers and crew to intervene.
Modi said India’s 1.4 billion people salute the captain and are praying for his well-being.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu described the Dubai flight rescue as “a chain of miracles with divine assistance” during a Torah study session focused on heroism.
Netanyahu hosted the Hoshana Rabba gathering Thursday evening in the Knesset sukkah, according to his office.
“The tradition of Jewish heroism tips the scales,” Netanyahu said. “What happened yesterday is a chain of miracles with divine assistance.”
His remarks followed the attack aboard the Dubai-to-Tel Aviv flight, where passengers and crew intervened before the aircraft landed safely in Saudi Arabia.
Rep. Mark Harris, R-N.C., praised the passengers and captain who helped stop the attack aboard FlyDubai Flight 1073, saying their courage sent a message to terrorists.
“The courage displayed aboard FlyDubai Flight 1073 is nothing short of extraordinary,” Harris wrote on X.
Harris singled out Israeli passenger Yaniv Hayun, saying he saw innocent people in danger and “acted without hesitation.”
“His bravery, alongside the actions of Captain Smit Machchhar and others on board, helped save 174 lives, including four Americans,” Harris wrote.
The State Department previously confirmed that four Americans were aboard the Dubai-to-Tel Aviv flight, which diverted to Saudi Arabia.
“God bless these heroes and the message they send to radicalized terrorists plotting attacks around the world,” Harris added. “Good will always triumph over evil.”
Israel is sending investigators to the United Arab Emirates to help determine whether anyone directed the co-pilot accused of trying to bring down the Dubai-to-Tel Aviv flight, a spokesman for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said.
David Mencer told “The Story” that Netanyahu confirmed the Omani suspect had been transferred to the UAE, allowing Israeli teams to join the UAE-led investigation.
“We'll get to know a whole lot more information now that he's in the UAE and we can join the investigation,” Mencer said.
Mencer also relayed a chilling account Netanyahu received from a passenger who entered the cockpit: The attacker was allegedly standing over the aircraft’s controls and using his feet to destroy them while attacking the captain.
“His objective was to bring down that airplane,” Mencer said.
The spokesman alleged the attack was intended to undermine the Abraham Accords and disrupt Israel’s election. He did not provide evidence supporting those claims or establish whether the suspect had been directed by Iran or another organization.
Investigators would examine the suspect’s motives, plans and possible connections, Mencer said.
A Boston native aboard the plunging Dubai-to-Tel Aviv flight held hands with an 11-year-old girl and prepared goodbye messages to her family as she feared she might not survive.
Mika Bauman, 25, a dual U.S.-Israeli citizen, described the terrifying ordeal to NBC News, saying passengers screamed as the aircraft suddenly descended during the cockpit attack.
“We didn't let go until Saudi Arabia, ” Bauman told the outlet.
Bauman said she could not see what was happening at the front of the aircraft but could tell it was angled toward the ground. She described intense pressure as the jet fell.
The flight eventually stabilized and landed safely in Saudi Arabia after passengers and crew intervened.
Bauman said she deleted the messages she had prepared for her family once the immediate danger passed, determined to believe she would make it home to Tel Aviv.
The attack remains under investigation, including whether it was terrorism-related.
Airlines need to look harder at the people inside the cockpit, an aviation security expert warned after the attack aboard the Dubai-to-Tel Aviv flight.
Arik Arad, founder of CYVIATION and former head of security for El Al at Ben Gurion Airport, said the incident should prompt stronger employee screening and closer attention to pilots’ mental health.
“I don't think that most of the airlines are actually aware of a potential threat that comes from the inside the cockpit,” Arad said.
He recommended psychological, behavioral and environmental assessments alongside pilots’ required medical exams and simulator training to identify stress or other problems.
Airlines, he argued, may be unwilling or unable to devote enough resources to monitoring pilots’ daily mental health.
Arad predicted the incident would lead to additional security procedures and regulations, including changes to employee background checks.
“I believe this will teach us all a lesson of how to actually examine pilots further,” he said.
Former Secretary of State Mike Pompeo praised Israeli passengers who intervened aboard the Dubai-to-Tel Aviv flight, saying their heroism helped avert a catastrophe.
“The attempted terrorist attack aboard the FlyDubai flight to Tel Aviv could have been absolutely catastrophic, if not for the heroism of the Israeli passengers on board,” Pompeo wrote on X.

articles.title_orig: The family of Renee Good files lawsuits over her death during Minneapolis ICE raids
articles.title_zh: The family of Renee Good files lawsuits over her death during Minneapolis ICE raids
articles.content_orig:
The family of Renee Good, from left; father Tim Ganger, mother Donna Ganger, brother Luke Ganger and brother Brent Ganger, listen during a news conference after the family sued the U.S. government and several immigration officials, Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026, in Minneapolis. Ellen Schmidt/AP hide caption
The family of Renee Good , the 37-year-old killed last January by a federal agent during the Trump administration's immigration enforcement surge in Minnesota, filed two civil lawsuits against the federal government Thursday.
One of the lawsuits, against the United States government itself, is essentially a wrongful death case, arguing that Jonathan Ross, the Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer who killed Good, violated his agency's own policies and the Fourth Amendment by using excessive force.
It is seeking damages for Good's family for the suffering she experienced in the final moments of her life. And also for her partner, Becca Good, who witnessed the killing. The lawsuit says she has suffered intense emotional distress from what she has experienced. Ross shot Renee Good several times in her car. At the time, federal officials claimed she had weaponized her vehicle, though video evidence contradicted that.
The other lawsuit is rarer, alleging that federal officials engaged in a conspiracy to interfere with the civil rights of people in Minnesota.
It argues that Good's death was the "predictable and intended product" of the immigration crackdown in the state and that Ross' actions were in furtherance of a "carefully planned, coordinated effort" to make Somali and Hispanic people the "object of aggression and abduction" and to silence the people "who observed, documented, and warned of that campaign."
In making that argument, the lawyers, with the firm Romanucci & Blandin, relied on the Ku Klux Klan Act of 1871, which was used to combat the terrorism wrought by the KKK during the Reconstruction era.
"I would say the second lawsuit is very unusual," Rachel Moran, a law professor at the University of St. Thomas, told NPR. "It was immediately striking to me because the Trump administration has been aggressively using conspiracy charges , including here in Minnesota, against people involved in protesting the administration's immigration tactics."
Moran said the lawyers in the Good lawsuits seem to be "turning that tactic on its head" by arguing that administration officials are involved in an illegal conspiracy themselves.
According to Ben Berkman, one of the lawyers representing Good's family, the first lawsuit is about what federal officers did to Renee Good on a Minneapolis street last winter. The second is about why those officers were on that street in the first place.
"It reaches the agent who fired those shots at Renee and it reaches every official who put him on the street that day," Berkman said. "No mask, no badge and no title in the administration puts anyone above that law."
Those federal officials include Ross, but also White House adviser Stephen Miller, former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, White House Border czar Tom Homan, and former Border Patrol Commander Gregory Bovino, among others. NPR reached out to the Department of Homeland Security for comment, but did not hear back.
In a statement, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said, "We intend to vigorously defend these baseless civil lawsuits."
The lawsuit also lists 10 federal agents who were also present at the scene as John Does, noting that the federal government has not released their identities and that they were wearing masks at the time of the killing.
The civil charges also underscore a lack of criminal charges . DHS has provided little public indication that it is investigating Good's death or the death of Alex Pretti at the hands of Border Patrol agents a few weeks later in Minneapolis. According to The Trace, a news site that focuses on gun violence, nine people have been killed by immigration agents since President Trump took office again last year.
A memorial for Renee Good, who was killed by federal agents in Minneapolis in January, remains in place at the site of her death, Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026, in Minneapolis. Ellen Schmidt/AP hide caption
At the state level in Minnesota, local officials have also not filed charges or released the findings of any investigation. In a statement, a spokesperson for Hennepin County, where Minneapolis is located, told NPR that state and local officials are reviewing the evidence and that they will "communicate transparently when a decision is reached."
At the press conference held Thursday, Good's family seemed frustrated at the inaction on all levels. Civil suits, like the ones filed by the family today, have the potential to hold entire institutions accountable rather than just individual actors.
"The fact that there's been no accountability, no investigation, no expression of condolence, no change in policy is completely mind-blowing," Brent Ganger, Good's brother, said. "We will not wait any longer. The time is absolutely now for accountability, for the deep damage done by ICE and others. We will not be quiet. We will not go away."
Brent and his mother, Donna Ganger, also testified before Congress last week at a hearing about fatal shootings by federal immigration officers.
In her first public appearance since the killing, Becca Good, Renee Good's partner, also spoke. She focused her words on who Renee was to her, calling her kind and loving, but also on what she has lost. Renee Good had three children, and Becca is still raising their youngest, a 6-year-old.
"This past August, I got ready to put our son in first grade. I bought him new shoes and a backpack and notebooks, pencil case, the whole nine yards. I went to Back To School Night on my own," Becca Good said. "She never missed a single moment. And this Halloween, it's our son's absolute favorite holiday. I'll take him trick or treating, without her hand in mine."
NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews. Anyone who makes such an offer or request is not an NPR employee and does not represent NPR.

In a recent interview with content creator Angelica Siciliani Fendi , Apple's vice president of hardware engineering Kate Bergeron revealed that the iPhone Duo's nano-texture cover layer above the inner display can be removed and replaced.
"It's actually replaceable, which is a really nice thing for the customer that you can peel off that layer and get a new one," said Bergeron.
In the U.S., customers who purchase AppleCare+ coverage for the iPhone Duo can get the cover layer replaced for $19, according to Apple's website . The cost to replace the cover layer without coverage has yet to be disclosed.
The cover layer helps to hide the crease in the middle of the foldable inner display. Bergeron said Apple did a "significant amount of engineering work" to ensure that this layer remains in good condition for as long as possible, but customers will have the option to replace it if it wears down or the crease becomes more visible over time.
Officially, the ability to replace the iPhone Duo's cover layer will likely be limited to Apple Stores and Apple Authorized Service Providers. It remains to be seen if customers will be able to easily remove the layer themselves.

articles.title_orig: ‘Verity’ To Seduce $55M+ Worldwide Opening As Box Office Braces For ‘Digger’ Impact – Global Preview
articles.title_zh: ‘Verity’ To Seduce $55M+ Worldwide Opening As Box Office Braces For ‘Digger’ Impact – Global Preview
articles.content_orig:
Editorial Director/Box Office Editor
Well, on the bright side of things, the autumn box office should continue at a great hum this weekend thanks to Amazon MGM Studios’ feature take on the Colleen Hoover thriller Verity , starring Dakota Johnson, Anne Hathaway and Josh Hartnett. The domestic outlook is $30 million-plus at 3,510 theaters, with the definite potential to overperform given how there’s walk-up business from Hoover-philes.
The Michael Showalter-directed thriller also has a shot at $20M-$25M in 70 offshore territories sans Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Vietnam and CIS in this suite, which would be a $50M-$55M global start. Previews stateside start Thursday on Verity at 2 p.m.
Meanwhile, light candles and say prayers for Warner Bros/Legendary Entertainment’s Tom Cruise -starring, Alejandro G. Iñárritu-directed Digger . Many are bracing for what could be one of Cruise’s lowest wide openings at the box office of the millennium. Warners believes the movie can get to $12M-$15M at 3,300 theaters; others believe it’d lucky to break $10M at the domestic box office.
Seventy-three foreign territories except Poland, Vietnam, Malaysia and Thailand (no China release) are expected to deliver another $15M-$20M abroad for Digger at 14,000+ screens, which would mean a $35M global start at the high end for the reported net $125M production (rumors suggest the movie cost much higher, between $140M-$150M).
Unlike the Dune franchise, Legendary didn’t co-finance Digger , but they did produce it. Previews start at 2 p.m. in North America, with tickets on sale in Imax, Dolby Cinema, VistaVision, PLFs and motion seats.
Digger was shot at Leavesden Studios with UK tax credits; the global marketing spend is approaching $100M. To say that the movie is divisive is an understatement, with some critics hailing the brilliance of the polemic movie and its Doctor Strangelove satire, while others were simply impatient watching it. Current Rotten Tomatoes critical score is 52%, and know that Cruise has had lower ratings (2017’s The Mummy was 15% Rotten with reviewers, and 2016’s Jack Reacher: Never Go Back was 37% Rotten). Warners in a last-minute marketing salvo is leaning into selling the controversy of the film with a final spot, this tweet having clocked 2.2 million views:
Decide for yourself. DIGGER – in theaters and IMAX FRIDAY. Tickets on sale now. https://t.co/Z1IpSpFnXd pic.twitter.com/e5ID4WUxbL
Back in his heyday as a star, Cruise posted low openings at the domestic box office in the single-digit range (i.e., the classic Rain Man opened to $7M in 1988 at 1,248 theaters and powered to $172.8M domestic), but those were different distribution days when movies opened small and played long. Post-2000, some of Cruise’s lowest North American opening have included the 2007 drama Lions for Lambs ($6.7M; $35M production cost), 2012’s Rock of Ages ($14.4M; $75M production cost), Jack Reacher ($15.2M and $60M production cost, though it spawned a Prime Video TV franchise) and 2017’s American Made ($16.7M; $60M net production).
RELATED: The 65 Movies That Have Made More Than $1 Billion At The Global Box Office
However, on a seismic bomb level, 2017’s The Mummy at $31.6M domestic opening/$172.6M worldwide wasn’t enough to save that $195M production, which finaled at $80.2M domestic, $409.2M WW. The arguments made for his spendy Mission: Impossible movies, particularly the last two, is that they’re bound to profit in their nth cycle (You gotta look at the overall library not just the individual movie, Paramount says in defending that franchise).
What positive things are there to say about Digger at this point? Domestic tracking in first choice climbed from a 2 since landing on tracking to a 7, which is the same as Cruise’s American Made and higher than Marty Supreme ($17.7M opening). Who wants to see this movie? Best first choice right now is men over 25, which is above the tracking figures for American Made and Marty Supreme .
RELATED: ‘Digger’ World Premiere Red Carpet Photos: Tom Cruise, Sandra Hüller, Riz Ahmed, Emma D’Arcy & More At London Premiere
Back to Verity. We hear U.S./Canada presales are behind It Ends With Us ($50M opening; $148.5M domestic final, $351.4M WW) , but that’s not a bad thing. That movie was Hoover’s most popular novel, and it opened when Blake Lively was in the mega-ether of Deadpool & Wolverine. Not to mention female audiences were intrigued by the percolating crisis between Lively and her co-star/director Justin Baldoni (fans were already deconstructing bad blood between them from red-carpet photos alone).
Hollywood went on a buying spree, snapping up Hoover tomes for the big screen. Two of them, Paramount’s Regretting You ($13.6M opening, $48.8M domestic, $90.4M WW) and Reminders of Him ($17.9M opening, $48.5M domestic, $89.2M WW) were all right in regards to their budgets, but not box office sensations. Verity is arguably Hoover’s second-most popular novel.
Like-for-like comps for Verity abroad are above The Drama ($9.4M international opening), lit thriller Where the Crawdads Sing ($12M) and Reminders of Him ($10M, though that was in 56 territories). The lit adaptation should do well in Europe, specifically Scandinavia, and we’re hearing advance ticket sales are really hot in Brazil, where Verity is above It Ends With Us. articles.title_orig: As Mortgage Rates Hit Highest Level Since 2023, Buyers Look at ARMs
articles.title_zh: As Mortgage Rates Hit Highest Level Since 2023, Buyers Look at ARMs
articles.content_orig:
Mortgage rates keep going up.
The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate was 7.28% this week, up from 7.03% last week, according to Freddie Mac data released Thursday. Mortgage rates have risen for six straight weeks, and this week brought the biggest one-week jump in nearly four years. Rates are now at their highest level since November 2023.
Turmoil in the bond market is driving rates higher. The 10-year Treasury yield has risen in recent months as investors worry that the Iran war and increased government spending could further stoke inflation and push the Federal Reserve toward higher rates for longer.
If you’re currently in the market for a home, the good news is you may be facing less competition from rate-sensitive buyers who are stepping back. But if you need a mortgage, the bad news is you will likely pay more in monthly costs than you would have just a few months ago.
But even with borrowing costs high – and potentially headed higher – a sub-7% mortgage rate may still be within reach for some buyers. The trade-off could be a riskier loan or a much bigger upfront payment.
Most home buyers opt for a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage because it typically offers lower monthly payments and predictable costs.
But it’s not the only option. Other types of mortgages may offer lower interest rates, potentially saving borrowers money over the life of the loan.
A 15-year mortgage typically has a lower interest rate than a 30-year mortgage, though monthly payments are significantly higher. Another option that is becoming increasingly popular lately: adjustable-rate mortgages (ARMs).
As of the latest data last week, “ARM loans, with rates around 80 basis points lower than fixed rate loans, accounted for 10.3% of applications, the highest share since October 2025,” according to Joel Kan, deputy chief economist at the Mortgage Bankers Association.
How are higher interest rates and rising prices affecting you?
But ARM loans, the mortgage products that helped fuel housing market risk in the lead-up to the 2008 financial crisis, are riskier than fixed-rate loans . They typically offer a lower fixed rate for five, seven or 10 years before resetting with market rates. If rates are higher when the fixed period ends, borrowers can be hit with sharply higher monthly payments.
“It may work well for some borrowers who are expecting to move or refinance in four or five years,” said Jeremy Luke, a divisional director at Chase Home Lending. “It may not work for all.”
Another way to get a lower mortgage rate is to take over someone’s existing mortgage as an assumable loan .
Not all home loans can be passed to a home buyer, but most government-backed loans, such as those from the Federal Housing Administration, the US Department of Veterans Affairs and the US Department of Agriculture, are assumable.
However, the approval process for an assumable mortgage can take longer. And because the buyer takes over only the seller’s remaining loan balance, they may need to bring significantly more cash to the table to cover the difference between that balance and the home’s purchase price.
The rate an individual buyer gets depends on more than market conditions. Lenders also consider factors such as the borrower’s credit score, debt-to-income ratio and down payment, said Jeff DerGurahian, head economist at loanDepot.
After shopping around, if you are unsatisfied with the rates you’ve been offered, it’s often possible to pay more up front in exchange for a reduced interest rate.
Permanent buydowns lower your interest rate for the life of the loan, whereas temporary buydowns, which can be cheaper, lower your rate for only the first few years.
But it’s important not to overdo it, DerGurahian said.
“You don’t want to put so much money down that you can’t do what you need to do to live in your house and live day-to-day,” he said.
Sometimes, the home’s seller or a builder can cover the cost of a rate buydown.
Builders are leaning more heavily on incentives to attract buyers to new construction, offering concessions such as mortgage rate buydowns and closing-cost credits. In September, 66% of builders reported using sales incentives, up from 63% in August and the highest share since December, according to the National Association of Home Builders’ sentiment survey.
A buyer should also understand the demand picture in their local market, said DerGurahian.
If it’s a buyer’s market, that means the supply of homes in that area exceeds demand, giving home buyers the upper hand. If a homeowner is motivated to sell, they may be willing to offer concessions to attract a buyer. If sellers have the upper hand in a local market, though, it’s less likely.
Certain buyers may have access to federal programs that can help them secure more favorable mortgage rates, including VA loans for eligible veterans and USDA loans for buyers purchasing homes in qualifying rural areas.
There are also banks and credit unions that offer relationship pricing or preferential rates.
For example, Chase occasionally runs “rate sales” where home buyers (and homeowners looking to refinance) can lock in discounted rates, Luke said.
Some banks, including Chase, also offer a discounted rate if customers move eligible deposits and investments into that bank, Luke added.
It pays to shop around. Experts generally recommend applying with at least three different mortgage lenders to make sure you’re getting a competitive rate. Compare the rates offered, closing costs and other fees to get a clearer picture of the total cost of each loan.
And you don’t necessarily have to worry about multiple credit checks dinging your score. To shop around for mortgages without hurting your credit, limit your search to a window of 14 to 45 days, according to Bankrate.

articles.title_orig: Diddy placed in solitary following NBC News report on his VIP prison life
articles.title_zh: Diddy placed in solitary following NBC News report on his VIP prison life
articles.content_orig:
Sean “Diddy” Combs has been placed in solitary confinement following an NBC News report on his VIP lifestyle inside prison, according to a source with knowledge of the matter.
The disgraced hip-hop mogul arrived at the Fort Dix federal prison in New Jersey in October after he was sentenced to 50 months behind bars for transporting people across state lines for sexual encounters.
Since then, he has spent thousands of dollars a month to bring his high-end lifestyle to the low-security prison, NBC News reported Tuesday in a story based on interviews with four men who spent time in the same unit as Combs.
They said he had no trouble acquiring contraband items such as cellphones and premium liquor, including Hennessy. He also pays several inmates who cook special meals for him, clean the toilet and shower areas before he uses them, do his laundry, make his bed and even give him Chinese-style massages.
“This is not some normal s--- you see in jail. This is some rich s---,” one of the sources said. “It looks crazy, but again, it’s Diddy.”
NBC News also obtained photos and videos inside the prison, which include video of Combs appearing to use a contraband cellphone.
Diddy appears to use cellphone in prison
After the report was published, Combs was removed from his dormitory-style quarters and placed in a special housing unit, better known as solitary confinement or the SHU, according to the source.
A Bureau of Prisons spokesperson would neither confirm nor deny that Combs was moved.
“For privacy, safety, and security reasons, we do not comment on the conditions of confinement for any incarcerated individual, including quarters assignment or whether a particular individual is the subject of allegations, investigations, or sanctions,” the spokesperson said.
TMZ was first to report that the Bad Boy Records founder was moved to solitary.
Federal prisons often transfer inmates to the special housing unit when they are the subjects of an investigation, experts say.
“We’d put people in the SHU while we were gathering evidence,” said Vito Maraviglia, a retired special investigator for the Bureau of Prisons who worked at Fort Dix in the late 1990s.
Maraviglia said the New Jersey prison is known as one of the cushiest in the federal prison system. It has segmented housing areas that are more difficult to monitor than at other facilities, making it easier for inmates to hide and use contraband items like cellphones.
“A high-profile guy like that, with all that money, I’m surprised they put him at a place like Fort Dix,” Maraviglia said.
Inmates placed in the SHU are locked in a cell with one other person for at least 23 hours a day, according to two men who spent time at Fort Dix. Inmates are allowed a book or two and a wind-up radio, the sources said, and they must wear an orange jumpsuit instead of the regular khaki uniform or gray sweatpants and shirts.
Meals are delivered in trays, but commissary access is restricted, and they are permitted to shower only a few days a week. The sources said they must otherwise wash up in a sink.
“It’s nasty down there,” one of the sources said.
It isn’t Combs’ first time in solitary confinement at Fort Dix. Last summer, he was placed in the special housing unit after he got into a fight with another inmate.
He was later kicked out of a drug treatment program at the prison but continued paying inmates to do a range of services for him, NBC News reported Tuesday.
The story prompted responses from people as varied as Combs’ longtime nemesis 50 Cent and the prominent attorney Gloria Allred, who represents a woman suing him for allegedly raping her more than 20 years ago. (Combs has denied the allegations, and the case is ongoing.)
“These serious allegations against Mr. Combs cry out for an immediate federal investigation and appropriate federal action including a prosecution if the allegations of having and using a cell phone while incarcerated can be proven beyond a reasonable doubt,” Allred said in a statement.
Other famous people have also received perks in prison, including Martha Stewart and Harvey Weinstein .
Combs’ trial last year centered on drug-fueled orgies he organized called “freak offs.” They involved male sex workers and his former girlfriends — including the singer Cassie — who filed a lawsuit against Combs alleging years of physical and sexual abuse. (The case was settled, with Combs denying any wrongdoing.)
The trial ended in a split verdict, with a New York jury finding him not guilty on the more serious charges of sex trafficking and racketeering charges that could have put him in prison for life.
Rich Schapiro is a reporter with the NBC News national security unit.

articles.title_orig: Exclusive | Friendly-faced California tech CEO arrested by feds for allegedly hiding $300M Chinese secret
articles.title_zh: Exclusive | Friendly-faced California tech CEO arrested by feds for allegedly hiding $300M Chinese secret
articles.content_orig:
Federal agents on Wednesday arrested a California tech CEO who’s accused of smuggling more than $300 million in restricted AI chips into China.
Greg Lui, 38, aka “Yiu Kong Lui,” of San Gabriel, faces a barrage of federal charges for allegedly selling Beijing a mountain of American-made AI graphics processors in violation of US laws, potentially threatening national security.
The California Post watched as the FBI and Department of Commerce agents arrested the high-flying tech boss in a stealth raid at the City of Industry headquarters of Earthmade Computers, a company Lui founded and runs, and which he allegedly used to conduct the profitable yet illegal scheme.
The biggest news, opinion and culture shaping California right now.
Agents tracked Lui as he drove a Tesla Cybertruck with a white wrap from his gigantic San Gabriel mansion to the Earthmade’s shiny offices in a tidy industrial park, handcuffing him at gunpoint soon after he arrived at work. Lui didn’t speak as he was placed in a vehicle to be taken in for processing.
AI is now used in nearly every aspect of modern warfare, and investigators said the advanced tech allegedly smuggled by Lui could’ve easily been put to use by the Chinese military.
“Protecting America’s national security means keeping our advanced Super Intelligence technology from being used to strengthen our adversaries’ military capabilities,” said First Assistant United States Attorney Bill Essayli.
“This defendant allegedly used false paperwork and shipments through third countries to smuggle more than $300 million in export-controlled computer servers to China,” Essayli added. We will aggressively prosecute those who put our national security at risk for profit.”
Federal prosecutors say Lui and his co-conspirators used Earthmade to buy and send sensitive AI tech into China from 2023 to 2024, without the required licenses issued by DOC that are meant to promote US foreign policy and protect national security.
Instead, they shipped these items to countries such as Malaysia and Singapore, where no licenses are required, and then illegally re-exported them to China.
The items in question were high-end computer servers, containing processors made by Nvidia Corp , a Santa Clara tech company specializing in AI. According to federal regulations, such tech could make significant contributions to Chinese armed forces.
As part of the alleged scheme, prosecutors say, Lui and his conspirators used fake documents to show the potentially dangerous AI tech would be going to destinations that did not require an export license in orders they placed with suppliers such as Nvidia.
After making these orders, Lui hired freight forwarding companies to ship the processors to Malaysia and Singapore . Once the servers arrived in these locations, Lui worked with his conspirators to reship the items to China.
From January 2024 to October 2024, Earthmade received more than $176 million from two Malaysia-based shipment companies as part of the scheme, according to court papers.
Prosecutors say Lui executed the scam knowing what he did was illegal, and they have the evidence to prove it.
For example, prosecutors say, Lui emailed a conspirator in January 2024 saying a Malaysian transshipment company wanted to buy 70 computer servers with the controlled AI tech. In the email, he noted the laws against the sale of such tech, according to court papers.
Later that month Lui purchased 27 of the servers for roughly $7.6 million and sent the servers from LA to Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. Two months later, one of Lui’s conspirators told a Malaysian official in an email that the servers had, in fact, been transshipped to China.
Prosecutors say Lui used a LA-based JP Morgan Chase account and Bank of America account to send and receive money to orchestrate the scheme.
Lui is charged with one count of conspiracy to violate the Export Control Reform Act , one count of smuggling and one count of conspiracy to commit money laundering. If convicted he faces up to 50 years in prison.
Before his arrest Lui lived a luxurious lifestyle, recently completing an extensive renovation of the 4,300-square foot mansion on Walnut Grove Avenue that he used to house numerous members of his extended family.
Federal agents were seen conducting a search of the massive spread Thursday, recording video and carrying evidence from the nine-bedroom, seven-bathroom home that has two stories and just got new stucco and windows, a fresh driveway and other upgrades.
The US DOC, the Defense Criminal Investigative Service and the FBI are investigating the case.
According to his LinkedIn page, Lui has an eight-year career in tech that began with a stint at Amplitude Tech Hosting Service, a Denver-based firm specializing in database colocation.
In 2021 he founded Earthmade Computer, which also handles database colocation, in addition to computer processor procurement and export, according to LinkedIn.
Before his tech run, Lui was a restauranter who specialized in ultra-spicy Sichuan Chinese food. In 2012 he co-founded of Duo-Pot in Arcadia, a Chinese hot pot and dry pot joint that sold spicy frog dishes before it closed in 2021, according to LinkedIn.

articles.title_orig: Following loss, Willson Contreras critical of Red Sox’ reliance on data and analytics
articles.title_zh: Following loss, Willson Contreras critical of Red Sox’ reliance on data and analytics
articles.content_orig:
NEW YORK — For the Red Sox, the playoffs had barely begun by the time the Yankees delivered a sledgehammer of shattering finality.
In two games, the Sox were outscored, 18-2, in the most lopsided Wild Card Series in the brief history of the best-of-three format. Their 9-0 blanking at the hands of Cam Schlittler and the Yankees in Game 1 was followed by a 9-2 slobberknocking in Game 2 that spelled the end of the series and the season.
How to make sense of the shellacking?
“It’s a good question. It’s different for everybody,” said Trevor Story. “You work your [butt] off all year, all offseason, and you get to this point, and this is what we play for. You play to win in the postseason, and to have it end [in Yankee Stadium] two times in a row is tough, and everyone will process that differently.”
For some players, there was appreciation of the zombie-like midyear return from the dead, a 15-game winning streak and 32-5 stretch unlike anything that most of the players had experienced. Yet the traces of those summer memories were clouded by the thrashing they’d just endured.
The Sox hit .117 (7 for 60) — the second-worst average by any team in any playoff series. Their .159 on-base percentage was the lowest. They barely had any runners in scoring position in the two games, and when they did, they literally did nothing, going 0 for 3 with nary a base runner.
Willson Contreras was in little mood for silver linings. At 34, he is their elder statesperson among position players. He was the team’s best hitter this year, hitting .275/.386/.516 with career highs in on-base and home runs (27). He is an influential clubhouse voice.
Despite playing through a number of injuries, he was their one source of offense Wednesday, going 2 for 2 with a homer and a pair of walks. His four times on base doubled the combined total of the rest of the lineup.
“We didn’t play good at all,” he said. “We didn’t pitch. We didn’t hit. And when you don’t have those two it’s tough to win. [The Yankees] played better than us.”
For Contreras, that straightforward analysis was the beginning of a critique of the Red Sox organization that sharpened as he continued.
“I’m really proud of this group, [but] whatever we did in the past stays in the past,” he said. “We have to get better for next year. In every aspect of the game, we have to get better. That’s the bottom line.”
How did an offense that was tops in the American League for a 60-game stretch (5.18 runs per game from June 25 through Aug. 31) regress to early-season form by staggering through September (an MLB-worst 2.96 runs per game) and then collapse in a brief postseason?
“That’s a good question. I’m not going to answer it because I don’t want to give my honest answer,” said Contreras. “We got eliminated. That’s the bottom line … We didn’t produce. We didn’t execute any part of the game. And that’s why we [lost].
“I know we had a really good stretch. I’m really proud of what we did in the past, like I said. We were able to turn the season around for sure, 100 percent, but that’s not enough. It’s not enough.”
Contreras suggested both specific areas in which the Sox needed to improve — for instance, controlling the running game of opponents — but also macro-level adjustments.
“It’s not enough when you have talent or you have data or you have computers telling you what to do. This is baseball and the data is here to help us,” he said. “But at the end of the day, you’re going to need experience and veteran guys to win games. There’s a lot of stuff that I would love to say but I’ll stay [with] that.”
Does Contreras believe the Sox are too data-reliant?
“If you watch the game,” Contreras responded incredulously, implying that the answer was obvious. “If you watch the game.”
Given that view, is there anything Contreras or other players can do to encourage the organization to evolve in its approach?
“I don’t know. I cannot make decisions,” he said. “The only thing that I can control is my part of the game … Making decisions about data, about all that stuff, we cannot do anything about it. Like I said, it’s here to help us. But at the end of the day, it’s not about data. It’s about executing the game plan.
“At the end of the day, we can talk, we can share ideas. I’m not making decisions and we’re not going to make decisions. We are employees. We get paid to play baseball, and we play to be out there on the field, to perform. That’s the bottom line.”
Despite his misgivings, Contreras — who had to waive his no-trade protection in order to complete his December trade from the Cardinals to the Red Sox — suggested he is content in the organization.
“I really had fun,” said Contreras, whose contract has one more guaranteed year, plus a team option for 2028. “This [was] my first season in Boston. I didn’t have any expectations coming up here when I got traded. I didn’t want to put anything in my mind.
“[But] I’m really proud [with] what I was able to do during the whole season,” he said. “But also, I’m proud of the team that we’ve got here and proud of everybody.”

articles.title_zh: Sony Brings AI Upscaling To The Base PS5
articles.content_orig:
Marvel’s Wolverine and Ghost of Yōtei are the first games to support Quick Spectral Super Resolution.
Sony Interactive Entertainment has added AI upscaling to the standard PS5. It's deploying patches for Marvel's Wolverine and Ghost of Yōtei today that make them the first games to support Quick Spectral Super Resolution (QSSR) through new graphics options. SIE said the tech delivers "notable improvements" to image detail and stability, adding that every PlayStation developer will be able to add QSSR to their games.
The company has offered PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR) upscaling on PS5 Pro since the higher-end version of the console arrived two years ago and it has continued to iterate on the tech . In a blog post, Sony says players and developers asked whether it was possible to bring a similar option to the less-powerful PS5.
QSSR stems from a project that Sony worked on with AMD. It says it's now able to offer AI upscaling on PS5 thanks to "a streamlined neural network architecture" and "a hand-tuned implementation that maximizes performance."
Mike Fitzgerald, head of technology at Wolverine developer Insomniac Games, said the tech "adds more pixel-level clarity and stability to our environments, bringing out extra detail amidst the busy streets of Madripoor, the dense alleyways of Shinjuku and many other areas across Logan's epic journey."
QSSR is arriving on Ghost of Yōtei on the same day Sucker Punch Productions is releasing a complete edition for that game with a story expansion and a roguelike mode that's akin to The Last of Us Part 2 's No Return . Folks who already own the game can upgrade for $15.

The co-main event on Saturday is Deiveson Figueiredo vs. Payton Talbott . Talbott is looking for a quality win to show he deserves to be in the Bantamweight title picture, while Figueiredo is just looking for any win to prove he still belongs here.

There’s also some veterans down there, too, with Marvin Vettori , Rafael dos Anjos and even Court McGee looking to remind us they are still here.
As always, there’s lots to bet on this card and we’ve got odds for all the fights below:
FIGHT STREAK RESULTS FOR UFC VEGAS 121!!! Get your picks in for UFC 332!!!
Well, we have two new leaders at the top. Rinya Nakamura took out a lot of folks last week, including previous leaders The Sassing Machine and MooseAlmighty. They have been overthrown by the conspiracy of Adam Wagner and Underdog Fan (who picked Deputy Hernandez and Yazmin Jauregui).
